name: Fluentd
summary: A CNCF graduated log collector that tags each event, routes it by tag through plugins, and buffers it until the destination accepts it.
intro: Fluentd is a daemon you run on every server (as a forwarder) or on a few central machines (as an aggregator). Every event it handles has three parts: a tag such as `nginx.access` that says where it came from, a timestamp, and a record, which is a JSON object. `<source>` blocks bring events in (tail a file, listen for HTTP or syslog, or accept the `forward` protocol from other Fluentd and Fluent Bit agents), `<filter>` blocks change or drop them, and `<match>` blocks send every event whose tag matches a pattern to an output. In front of each output sits a buffer: events collect into chunks, in memory or in files on disk, and a chunk is sent when it is full or its time slot closes. If the destination is down, Fluentd retries with exponential backoff, by default for up to 72 hours.

Its docs describe it as C underneath with a thin Ruby layer, and almost everything is a plugin: more than 1,000 external plugins are published as Ruby gems. Because of Ruby’s global interpreter lock one process uses about one CPU core, so busy hosts run several worker processes. Fluentd is free under Apache 2.0, with no paid edition; ClearCode maintains it and ships the `fluent-package` installers, and sells support. Its sibling Fluent Bit, written in C, does a similar job in about 450 KB of memory against Fluentd’s 60 MB or more, and speaks the same `forward` protocol, so the two can be mixed in one pipeline.
strengths: Tag-based routing keeps one config readable with many inputs and outputs: a `<match>` pattern decides where each kind of event goes
Retries with backoff ride out long outages, and since v1.19 file buffers move chunks that still fail to a backup directory instead of throwing them away
A very large plugin catalogue; `fluent-package` bundles outputs for S3, Kafka, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Prometheus, plus an OpenTelemetry (OTLP) plugin
Vendor-neutral and fully Apache 2.0 under the CNCF, with LTS packages: the v6 LTS series is supported until the end of 2027
limits: Heavier than its alternatives: more than 60 MB per process plus a Ruby runtime and gem dependencies. The Fluent Bit docs note that cloud providers have switched from Fluentd to Fluent Bit
Ruby’s global interpreter lock limits one process to about one CPU core; the single-process tuning guide covers up to about 5,000 messages a second, beyond that you configure `multi workers`
A memory buffer loses whatever it holds if Fluentd crashes; only a file buffer survives a restart, and you have to choose it per output
Built for logs: metrics and traces only arrive through plugins, unlike the OpenTelemetry Collector, which handles all three natively
Most plugins are external gems maintained outside the core project, so their quality and release pace vary

snippet.title: Tail an nginx log, tag it, and ship hourly files to S3 through a disk buffer
source: pos_file /var/log/fluent/nginx-access.pos   # remembers how far it has read
@type file                 # survives restarts; @type memory would not
timekey_wait 10m           # wait for late events before uploading

sections.intro: All five read from many sources, change data in flight and write it to many destinations. They differ in runtime, in the shape of data they were built around, and in who steers them.

sections.title: Fluentd or Fluent Bit?
sections.intro: Both are CNCF graduated projects under the Fluentd umbrella, both are Apache 2.0, and both can act as a forwarder or an aggregator. Fluent Bit started in 2014 as a lightweight processor for embedded Linux and gateways.

rows.label: Dependencies
values: A Ruby gem that depends on other gems
None, unless a plugin needs one

rows.label: Signals
values: Logs, metrics, traces and profiles; native OTLP in and out

notes: Figures from the Fluent Bit manual’s “Fluentd and Fluent Bit” page. Pick Fluentd when you need a plugin only it has; otherwise Fluent Bit is the lighter default for a per-node agent.

story: By 2011 a typical web company had logs in many formats on many servers, and wanted them in many places: files, databases, Hadoop, search engines. Every new pair of source and destination meant another script. Sadayuki Furuhashi, co-founder of Treasure Data, a cloud service for big data, made the first commit to Fluentd in June 2011 to build what the project calls a “Unified Logging Layer”: one place that collects events and hands them to whatever needs them.

As maintainer Kiyoto Tamura put it in 2014, with M inputs and N outputs there are M×N possible paths for log data; with a plugin for each input and each output, you need only M+N. Records became JSON, picked because almost everything can read it, not because it is fast.

Fluentd joined the CNCF in November 2016 and in April 2019 became its sixth graduated project, after Kubernetes, Prometheus, Envoy, CoreDNS and containerd. Its C sibling Fluent Bit, begun in 2014 by Eduardo Silva in the same team, has since replaced Fluentd at several cloud providers. ClearCode maintains Fluentd today, and in 2023 its `fluent-package` installers replaced Treasure Data’s `td-agent`.

choices.choice: Every event is a tag, a time and a JSON record
choices.why: JSON was chosen for how widely it is understood: databases and Hadoop could take it as it was. The tag let Fluentd route events without looking inside them.
With an input plugin per source and an output plugin per destination, connecting M sources to N destinations takes M+N pieces instead of M×N custom paths.

choices.choice: A buffer in front of every output
choices.why: Destinations go down. Collecting events into chunks that wait in a queue, in memory or on disk, and retrying with backoff keeps a slow or failed backend from losing logs or stalling the inputs.
